name: Technology Evaluation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Beyond the Whitepaper: A Framework for Evaluating Whether Blockchain Actually Helps
lesson.summary: A disciplined technology evaluation asks a small set of grounded questions, does multiple parties need write access, is a trusted intermediary genuinely the bottleneck, is immutability worth its costs, before layering on cost-benefit analysis, rather than starting from enthusiasm for the technology.
lesson.body:
Almost every chapter in this course up to this point has assumed blockchain is at least a candidate solution and explored how it works or how to govern it. This chapter asks a more basic question: for a given problem, is it actually the right tool at all? Technology evaluation is the discipline of answering that question with evidence rather than with enthusiasm, and it draws directly on evidence-based evaluation and on recognizing where a technology sits on the hype cycle covered earlier in the course.

A useful evaluation starts with a short sequence of grounded questions rather than a long list of features. Do multiple independent parties genuinely need to write to a shared record, or would one trusted party recording data on behalf of everyone else work just as well? If a single party could legitimately run the database, and the only reason to avoid that is a mild, general preference for decentralization rather than an articulable trust problem, a blockchain is very likely solving a problem that does not exist. Is there a specific, named intermediary whose current role creates cost, delay, or a conflict of interest that participants can point to concretely, or is "cutting out the middleman" more of a slogan than a diagnosed problem? Is the record's integrity actually load-bearing, meaning something bad and specific happens if a party could quietly alter history, or would ordinary access logging and legal contracts provide the same practical assurance at a fraction of the operational cost? Immutability, as the GDPR chapter made clear, is not a free feature; asking whether a use case truly needs it, rather than assuming more permanence is always better, is itself part of a rigorous evaluation.

The hype cycle matters here because the same underlying technology proposal reads very differently depending on when in the cycle it is being pitched. A proposal made near the peak of inflated expectations tends to arrive with confident claims and thin evidence, riding organizational enthusiasm rather than demonstrated results; a proposal made after the trough of disillusionment, once the initial hype has burned off, is more likely to come with sober, specific evidence because the surviving use cases are the ones that had to prove themselves. Evidence-based evaluation means consciously discounting for where on that curve you currently are, actively seeking out disconfirming evidence and documented failures alongside the vendor's success stories, rather than treating enthusiasm as a substitute for a track record.

Cost-benefit analysis is the quantitative backbone that turns these qualitative judgments into a decision. The benefits side has to include not just the theoretical value of disintermediation or tamper evidence, but the realistic, evidenced value given the maturity of the specific implementation. The cost side has to include far more than licensing or infrastructure: integration with legacy systems, the change management and stakeholder buy-in effort covered in the previous chapters, ongoing governance overhead for any consortium involved, and the opportunity cost of not building a simpler alternative, a well-designed database with strong contracts and audit logging, in the same amount of time. A technology evaluation that produces a real number for both sides, even a rough one, is far more useful than a qualitative sense that blockchain "seems appropriate," and it is the analytical foundation the technology readiness level, vendor assessment, and decision framework chapters that follow will all build on.
